analysis.one_liner: A constitutional amendment saying only natural persons have constitutional rights, letting Congress and states regulate corporations.
analysis.headline: Senator Jon Tester's amendment to limit constitutional rights to people rather than corporations drew no cosponsors and died in the Senate Judiciary Committee without a hearing or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill proposed a constitutional amendment stating that the rights in the Constitution belong to natural people, not to corporations, limited liability companies, or other corporate entities. It would also let Congress and state legislatures regulate those corporate entities as they see fit. Because changing the Constitution requires two-thirds of both chambers of Congress and approval by three-fourths of the states, it was a long-shot measure aimed at reining in corporate influence, especially in elections.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary voters and citizens. Under the bill's sections 1 and 2, constitutional rights would belong to natural persons only, and terms like "people," "person," and "citizen" would no longer include corporations [S3]. That would let elected representatives limit corporate money in elections and regulate corporate conduct — advertising, labor practices, environmental rules — without courts striking the rules down as violations of corporate constitutional rights [S3]. Section 3 spells out that corporations would be subject to whatever regulation Congress and state legislatures determine to be reasonable [S3]. Small candidates and grassroots groups would face less competition from unlimited corporate political spending, though the bill text does not mention elections directly — its subjects cover elections, campaign regulation, and political advertising [S1].

how_it_helps.text: Declares that constitutional rights belong to natural persons and that corporations, LLCs, and other corporate entities are excluded from the Constitution's terms 'people,' 'person,' and 'citizen,' undoing the legal doctrine of corporate personhood.

Gives Congress and state legislatures explicit authority to regulate corporate entities as they determine reasonable, so democratically passed rules on corporate conduct could not be voided by courts on the ground that a corporation's constitutional rights were violated.

The bill's listed subjects — elections, political campaign regulation, and political advertising — signal its main target: corporate influence in politics, including the corporate campaign spending that courts have protected as free speech.

analysis.who_pays: Corporations, LLCs, and their owners and executives. They would lose the ability to invoke constitutional rights — free speech, due process, protections against searches — in court, and would become subject to whatever regulation legislators choose to impose [S3]. Wealthy donors and business interests that currently benefit from corporate political spending would face new limits if lawmakers used the authority.

drawbacks.text: The wording is extremely broad. Section 2 excludes corporations from every constitutional term for 'person,' not just campaign-finance contexts, which could strip constitutional protections from unions, nonprofits, and even media companies — businesses that publish newspapers — unless courts or lawmakers drew careful lines.

The amendment path is arduous and, as drafted, it delegated the scope of regulation to whatever Congress and state legislatures determine 'reasonable' at a given time, with no floor of guaranteed protections, leaving corporate rights fully dependent on the political winds.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit — restoring the ability of elected governments to regulate corporate conduct and corporate money in elections without courts overriding them on constitutional grounds — is real and widely sought by campaign-finance reformers. But the bill as written goes much further than campaign finance: it removes all constitutional standing for corporate entities of every kind, including unions, advocacy nonprofits, and news organizations, and leaves them entirely at the mercy of whatever a legislature finds reasonable. A more carefully targeted amendment could have limited the harm; this one traded precision for reach.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the Senate Judiciary Committee for the entire two-year Congress and never received a hearing, a markup, or a vote.

narrative.text: Senator Jon Tester introduced the bill on March 11, 2019, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee the same day.
No other senator signed on as a cosponsor.
The Judiciary Committee took no further action for the rest of the 116th Congress, which ended January 3, 2021, so the bill never reached the Senate floor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Corporations and the interests that fund them. They keep the full set of constitutional protections the amendment would have stripped away, and nothing changed for anyone else because the bill never left committee.

for.name: Sen. Jon Tester
for.role: U.S. Senator from Montana; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the constitutional amendment and got it referred to the Judiciary Committee; no colleague joined him as a cosponsor.

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee (Chair Lindsey Graham)
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred; never scheduled a hearing or markup
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after it was referred on March 11, 2019, letting it die in committee at the end of the 116th Congress.

against.name: The other 99 sitting senators
against.role: None signed on as a cosponsor
against.what_they_did: Declined to cosponsor, leaving the bill with no bipartisan or even same-party backing that could have pressured the committee to act.

sides.party_line_note: There is no vote record to measure: the bill had a single Democratic sponsor, zero cosponsors from either party, and never reached the floor.

industries.note: The amendment would end corporate entities' ability to claim constitutional rights in court and would make them subject to whatever regulation Congress and the states impose. Their interest in stopping it was keeping those protections, which shield their political spending and their resistance to regulation — the opposite of what backers of the bill wanted for the public.

industries.industry: Corporate political spenders and campaign advertisers
industries.note: The bill's subjects include elections, campaign regulation, and political advertising. Corporate money in elections currently enjoys First Amendment protection; the amendment would let legislators restrict it, which its business opponents had every reason to resist.
